note: Second research pass. First batch (2026-09-01.json) was rejected as too AI-agent-news heavy. Deliberately shifted axis to browser platform features and hands-on frontend engineering - the biggest gap in a 182-article corpus saturated with Claude Code, agents and Next.js.

topics.title: Three.js Ships WebGPU by Default Now. Here Is What the Migration Actually Breaks
topics.whyTrending: WebGPU hit baseline in every major browser; Three.js r171+ ships a production WebGPU renderer with ~95% coverage and automatic WebGL2 fallback for the rest. 30-50% gains on dense scenes. The blog has 182 articles and zero on 3D or graphics despite three.js being a project dependency.

topics.title: Interop 2026: The Browser Features That Quietly Became Safe to Use
topics.whyTrending: Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, Bocoup and Igalia pushed cross-document View Transitions, popover anchor positioning and a usable WebGPU baseline past 90% WPT pass rate inside one quarter. A sourced 'what is genuinely safe now vs what still needs a fallback' reference is highly linkable and evergreen.

topics.title: Scroll-Driven Animations Are at 82%. The Progressive Enhancement Pattern That Makes That Fine
topics.whyTrending: animation-timeline / scroll() / view() are Chromium and Safari only; Firefox 152 still keeps it behind a flag, so it is technically not Baseline. The correct pattern - author the finished state as the default and layer motion on top - is exactly the discipline most React scroll-animation code violates. First-hand material from this blog's own LCP fix.

topics.title: Speculation Rules: Native Prerendering That Beats Your Router's Prefetch
topics.whyTrending: A browser-native way to prefetch and prerender likely next navigations, no framework required, and it pairs directly with View Transitions. Nothing on the blog covers it, and it competes head-on with the Next.js-specific navigation work already published.

topics.title: CSS Anchor Positioning in Production, Fallbacks Included
topics.whyTrending: Firefox 147 shipped in January 2026 and tipped the core properties into Baseline, but support is still uneven and it is nowhere near as safe as :has() or container queries. Tooltips, dropdowns and popovers without a positioning library is a concrete win, and the fallback story is where every tutorial stops.

topics.title: Five Font Families, One CLS Problem: What Web Fonts Really Cost
topics.whyTrending: next/font hides the complexity until you have five families swapping at different moments and a CLS score you cannot explain. Font metric overrides, size-adjust, and when display:swap is the wrong default. Written from a real audit of this blog with before/after numbers.

topics.title: Frontend i18n That Does Not Turn Into Technical Debt
topics.whyTrending: Localization reaches routing, bundle splitting, deployment and content ownership, and badly designed setups compound with every feature. Genuine first-hand angle: this blog shipped a Polish locale, then had to redirect all of it away because the translations became unmaintainable.

topics.title: A Content Security Policy You Can Actually Ship on Next.js
topics.whyTrending: Nonces, strict-dynamic, and why almost every Next.js CSP example on the internet is either unsafe-inline or broken in the App Router. The blog covers supply-chain and agent security heavily but has nothing on browser-side security headers.

topics.title: Web Workers and OffscreenCanvas: Buying Back Your INP Budget
topics.whyTrending: INP is sampled more strictly under the 2026 measurement change, and the main-thread work most teams never move off it is parsing, diffing and canvas rendering. Practical, code-heavy, and links naturally to the existing INP article without repeating it.

topics.title: Your 3D Hero Section Costs Two Seconds of LCP. Measure It Before You Ship It
topics.whyTrending: WebGPU adoption in new 3D-shipping apps jumped from ~8% to 65% in two years, and almost none of that content budgets for Core Web Vitals. Bridges the graphics and performance halves of the blog, which currently do not touch.
